summary:
Crashfall is a top-down Mars outpost builder designed as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Players crash-land on the Martian surface and must rebuild a dead outpost by placing modules, waiting for construction to complete, and physically wiring power from solar panels to a central reactor. Rather than abstracting power into a menu, the game makes every connection tangible: cables stretch like rubber bands across the dust and snap back if released on empty ground, construction states hide modules and their sockets until built, solar panels continuously re-aim at the reactor, and placement rules forbid building too close to the reactor — forcing the same spatial and power trade-offs real mission planners face.

It addresses the challenge by letting students experience competing outpost demands — power generation, construction time, spatial constraints — rather than reading about them. Real NASA Mars data (sol length, solar irradiance at 586 W/m², gravity) drives the day cycle and panel output, grounding the fiction in fact.

It matters because it turns abstract mission-planning decisions into a felt, playable lesson — the kind of intuitive understanding that sparks the next generation of astronauts and engineers.
details:
What it does / How it works

Crashfall is a top-down, diegetic Mars outpost builder. The player crash-lands on the Martian surface and must rebuild a dead station by placing modules, waiting for them to construct, and physically wiring power from solar panels back to a central reactor.

The core loop is:

  1. Place a module on the station grid — but not too close to the reactor (rejected placement, no cost lost).
  2. Wait for construction — the module and its wire socket stay invisible and non-interactable until built.
  3. Wire the module to the reactor — grab a cable, drag it across the dust. The wire stretches infinitely like a rubber band; release on empty ground and it snaps back elastically to its origin; release on a valid plug and the connection holds.
  4. Power flows — solar panels continuously rotate to face the reactor, and real NASA Mars data scales their output to ~43% of Earth-equivalent.

Everything is felt rather than read: no menu bars, no abstract power numbers. The wiring is the game.

Benefits

  • Teaches systems thinking. Players learn that outpost survival is a trade-off between power, space, and time — not a checklist.
  • Accessible to students. No prior base-builder experience needed; the tutorial points at the action, not the screen edge.
  • Runs offline. Live NASA imagery is fetched when available, with bundled fallbacks so the trainer works in classrooms without internet.
  • Open source. Fully open code, so educators can fork it, reskin it for lunar scenarios, or extend the module set.

Intended impact

The official challenge asks students to experience the decisions that determine mission success — not memorize facts about them. Crashfall makes those decisions tactile: a rejected placement stings, a snapped-back wire costs a second, a solar panel that produces half what you expected forces you to re-plan. That felt understanding is what turns curiosity into the next generation of mission planners, engineers, and astronauts. We want a middle-schooler to play for ten minutes and walk away knowing why power routing matters on Mars.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

  • Engine: Godot 4.6 (MIT-licensed)
  • Language: GDScript
  • Systems built: CharacterBody2D player with plug/pickup mechanics, TileMapLayer station grid with per-tile collision, custom wire-drag system with elastic snap-back tweens, animation-driven sprite state machine, scene-switching cutscene → crash → gameplay flow with audio cues.
  • NASA data: NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet (sol length 88,775 s, solar irradiance 586 W/m², gravity 3.73 m/s²) drives gameplay constants; APOD API with bundled fallback for the crash cutscene backdrop.
  • Hardware: Developed on standard laptops; no specialized hardware required.
  • Version control: Git (public repository).

How the project is creative

Most base-builders abstract power into a HUD number. We made it physical. The wire is a rubber band you can stretch across the screen and let snap back. Construction hides the module and its socket until it's real. Solar panels turn to face the reactor in real time. The tutorial doesn't sit in a corner — it tracks the object you're acting on. Every mechanic is diegetic: the game shows its rules through motion, not text.

Factors the team considered

  • Feasibility over scope. We chose four deep mechanics (construction gating, physical wiring, solar aiming, placement constraints) over twenty shallow ones. Every mechanic ships in the demo.
  • Demo reliability. API calls are wrapped with bundled fallbacks — the demo never breaks on stage or in a classroom without Wi-Fi.
  • Educational framing. We tuned the tutorial to be predictive (points at the object you'll act on) rather than descriptive (walls of text), because student retention comes from doing, not reading.
  • Asset licensing. All third-party art, sound, and tilesets are used under their free/commercial licenses and credited in CREDITS.md, so the project is redistributable.
  • Extensibility. The module system is data-driven, so a classroom can add lunar modules, greenhouse mechanics, or radiation shielding without touching core code.
  • Accessibility. Simple controls, readable UI, no fail state that punishes exploration — students can experiment without fear.
